prompt.brief: Design a serverless event-driven platform that accepts versioned events, routes them to independent consumers, supports retries and ordering where needed, and remains observable under bursty workloads.
successSignals: Define event envelopes, schemas, ownership, delivery guarantees, ordering keys, replay, consumer checkpoints, and idempotent side effects.
Separate ingress, routing, queues, workers, and durable state; isolate noisy tenants and apply backpressure, quotas, and dead-letter policies.
Explain fan-out, deduplication, poison events, schema evolution, partial consumer failure, and replay without duplicating business effects.
Cover authorization, encryption, auditability, tracing, cost controls, and degraded operation when workers or downstream systems fail.

functional: Publish validated events, route them by type/tenant/key, invoke independent consumers, and expose delivery, retry, and processing status.
Support ordered partitions where required, fan-out subscriptions, scheduled events, dead-letter inspection, replay, and consumer versioning.
Make side effects idempotent, preserve event lineage, enforce producer/consumer authorization, and recover after queue or worker outages.
nonFunctional: Deliver ordinary events to healthy consumers with p95 under one second while exposing lag and freshness explicitly.
Scale to 1M events per second and thousands of consumers without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

dataFlow.title: Accept Trigger functions from events
dataFlow.description: The Serverless event-driven platform gateway authenticates the caller, validates the request, applies tenant policy and idempotency, then routes it to the owning service.

dataFlow.title: Commit the durable state
dataFlow.description: The producer validates and durably accepts the event with its idempotency identity before acknowledgement.

dataFlow.title: Publish the domain event
dataFlow.description: A durable outbox publishes committed Serverless event-driven platform events; consumers deduplicate by event ID and track offsets.

dataFlow.title: Build the read model
dataFlow.description: Partitioned workers consume Serverless event-driven platform events, update the serving projection, and expose lag or watermark metadata.

dataFlow.title: Serve and recover asynchronously
dataFlow.description: Serving reads use the Serverless event-driven platform projection; replay, repair, export, and slow work remain off the request path.

architecture.title: Design an event-driven system that triggers functions based on events, processes messages asynchronously, and integrates with multiple cloud services. reference architecture
architecture.summary: The authoritative state records Trigger functions from events; asynchronous workers build serving projections while Cloud Functions for event handlers, Eventarc for event routing, Pub/Sub for messaging stays isolated from the request path.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the accepted domain mutation strongly consistent; make derived projections explicitly eventually consistent.
Use idempotency keys, conditional writes, event IDs, and resource versions so retries are safe.
Return version and observedAt so clients can reason about projection freshness and convergence.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Serverless event-driven platform by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Serverless event-driven platform work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Serverless event-driven platform projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable projection or a domain-safe degraded response when asynchronous dependencies fail.
Retain durable Serverless event-driven platform records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure domain latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and source-to-projection correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.

rubric.description: The answer defines event schemas, routing, delivery, scale, durability, replay, and failure contracts.
Entities and topic/partition keys support event delivery, consumer state, replay, authorization, and lifecycle changes.
Partitioning, cache behavior, queues, backpressure, and hot-key handling are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded reads, and observability protect committed state.
The candidate can explain Serverless event-driven platform consistency, push/pull, managed services, and the scale boundary.
